title: SYSK Selects: Why do men have nipples?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally aired January 2017 era, republished Aug 2017) hosted as a Saturday pick by Chuck. The hosts explore why men have nipples: the generally accepted explanation that all embryos develop mammary tissue before sexual differentiation, and that male mice and humans lose or keep it differently. They cover the Yale mouse study on the Pth-related protein (PTHrP), chromosomes and sexual dimorphism, male lactation (galactorrhea/galacteria), witch's milk in newborns, prolactin and fathers, a 2002 Sri Lanka case of a man breastfeeding his daughters, starvation-induced lactation in Japanese POW camps, the Aka pygmy tribe's involved fathering, Darwin's idea of ancestral male breastfeeding, male breast cancer, and supernumerary nipples. The episode closes with TV show promo for the Science Channel series and listener mail about PCOS.

segments.title: Rerun introduction by Chuck
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Selects rerun about why men have nipples, explaining it came from an earlier January episode, and the show's opening banter.

segments.title: Chromosomes and sexual development
segments.summary: The hosts explain that humans share 22 of 23 chromosome pairs regardless of sex, with XX and XY determining sex, and that sexual dimorphism is shaped in development and at puberty. Chuck shares an anecdote about a dog's nipples.

segments.title: Male mice and the PTHrP protein
segments.summary: The hosts cite the generally accepted explanation: most male mammals have nipples, with exceptions such as male platypuses. A Yale study found a protein (PTHrP) that in male mice destroys mammary tissue before birth. Humans also develop mammary tissue and milk lines before sexual traits, so males and females start with the same setup until hormones diverge at puberty. The default setting is female.

segments.title: Male lactation and estrogen
segments.summary: Men can potentially lactate if exposed to estrogen. Fetal exposure to maternal prolactin can cause witch's milk in newborns of both sexes, which usually lasts a couple of weeks. Galactorrhea is spontaneous lactation in adult men, linked to low testosterone and relatively high estrogen.

segments.title: Fathers, starvation, and breastfeeding cultures
segments.summary: Prolactin rises in fathers after birth and repeated nipple stimulation may trigger milk. A 2002 Sri Lanka case involved a man who breastfed his daughters after his wife died. Japanese POW camp prisoners who were starving sometimes lactated. The Aka pygmy tribe's fathers are very involved, and gender roles are interchangeable. Darwin raised the idea that early men may have breastfed.

segments.title: Why men don't breastfeed and cultural monogamy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why men do not routinely breastfeed despite having the equipment, suggesting evolution favored women doing it for millennia. They speculate that with more monogamous cultures, men might eventually breastfeed. Chuck mentions he was not breastfed.

segments.title: Male breast cancer and extra nipples
segments.summary: Men can get breast cancer, which is rare but occurs; about 2,000 American men were diagnosed in 2012 (figure as stated in transcript). The hosts consider whether nipples might be a flaw. They discuss supernumerary nipples, which are more common in males and on the left side, appearing in about one in forty newborns.

segments.title: Closing and further reading
segments.summary: Hosts point listeners to the HowStuffWorks article on male nipples and mention the Science Channel TV show.

segments.title: Science Channel television show promo
segments.summary: Promo for the Stuff You Should Know TV show on Science Channel, premiering January 9 after Idiot Abroad, with episodes on iTunes.

segments.title: Listener mail: PCOS and mustaches
segments.summary: A listener named Kayla writes about polycystic ovarian syndrome, which causes excess hair growth and infertility, and asks for awareness, referencing the Polycystic Association of Australia.
